sentences: Close your eyes and remember a significant moment from your childhood.
The image comes back to you, clear, colorful, with its sounds and emotions.
You feel like you're replaying a recorded scene, true to reality.
This feeling is one of the great illusions of the human mind.
Because memory does not work at all like a camera that archives the past to reproduce it intact.
It works like a storyteller: with each recollection, it reconstructs the story — and in doing so, modifies it.
The work of psychologists over the past several decades leaves little doubt.
Memory is not an object stored in a drawer that you can take out unchanged.
It is a reconstruction, done in the moment, based on fragments.
The brain retains a few central elements and fills in the gaps — with logic, expectations, and information acquired since.
The most troubling thing is that this reconstruction work is invisible to us: we do not feel the stitching between what was lived and what is invented.
The reconstructed memory presents itself with the same clarity, the same certainty, as the exact memory.
A researcher has demonstrated this fragility through famous experiments.
By cleverly suggesting false details to adults, she managed to make them 'remember' events that never happened: getting lost as a child in a shopping mall, spilling a bowl at a wedding.

Not only did the subjects adopt these false memories, but they also enriched them with spontaneous details, defended them emotionally, and often refused to believe, upon revelation, that they had been deceived.
We are not reliable guardians of our own history.
The consequences far exceed mere laboratory curiosity.
For a long time, the justice system treated eyewitness testimony as the ultimate proof: 'I saw it with my own eyes.'
We now know that a sincere witness, absolutely certain, can be gravely mistaken — and innocent people have been convicted based on such memories, only to be exonerated much later.

In a more everyday context, these mechanisms explain those unsolvable family disputes where everyone swears by their version: two people remember the same scene in incompatible ways, and both are acting in good faith.
Neither is lying.
Their memories have simply constructed two different narratives.
Should we then despair of our memory, considering it a fabric of inventions?
That would be an exaggeration in the other direction.
Essentially, it serves us faithfully: it retains the meaning, the main points, what matters for action.
It sacrifices the accuracy of details, but this 'unfaithfulness' may have a useful role — a flexible memory that constantly reorganizes, adapts better than a fixed recording.
The lesson is therefore not distrust, but humility.
The next time you are absolutely certain of a memory, remember that this very certainty proves nothing.
Your memory is a talented storyteller.
It does not seek to deceive you; it is simply doing its job, which has never been to tell the whole truth.

sentences: When data collection is mentioned, a common response is, 'I have nothing to hide.'
This comes from an understandable intuition, but it is based on a misunderstanding.
The question is not whether we have secrets.

The time at which we connect.
Daily commutes.

When gathered, they paint a very precise picture: work schedules, a probable state of health, family situation, beliefs, financial capacity, and sometimes a moment of vulnerability.
This profile has value, and that is why it is created.
Its uses are not all concerning — a better-suited service can sometimes be pleasant.
But some raise real questions: prices that vary according to the buyer's profile, credit offers targeted at people in difficulty, political ads addressed differently based on presumed sensitivities.
Another problem is the duration.

European law offers real protections: consent, right of access, right to erasure.
They are useful, but rarely used, as the interfaces make refusal tedious.

sentences: There is a common confusion in ecological discussions: people put gestures with effects that differ by a factor of one hundred on the same level.
Turning off the light when leaving a room is a good habit.
But in terms of emissions, it cannot be compared to a long-haul flight.
The available analyses provide fairly stable orders of magnitude for a European household.
What weighs the most are, in no particular order: air travel, the daily use of a personal car, heating a poorly insulated home, and food — particularly red meat.
What weighs significantly less includes: plastic bags, straws, letting tap water run for a few seconds, and lighting.
This does not mean that small gestures are useless.
They have a value of habit and consistency, and some have other benefits — plastic pollution is a real problem, even if its climate impact is low.

But it is discouraging, and a bit unfair, to place a disproportionate guilt on households for marginal gestures, while structural decisions — such as housing insulation, transport options, and urban planning — largely depend on public policies and businesses.
The practical conclusion is rather liberating.

It's better to focus your efforts on two or three truly important levers — reducing air travel, insulating your home, changing how you move around daily, adjusting your diet — rather than spreading yourself thin over twenty micro-gestures.
And there is one last lever, often forgotten: the voice.
A citizen who votes, writes, or supports a local project carries more weight than perfectly sorting their waste.

sentences: False information spreads quickly, and it spreads even better when it provokes strong emotions: outrage, fear, anger.
This is actually the first warning sign.
Any information that makes us react immediately deserves a few extra seconds of skepticism.
It's no coincidence: the most shared content is the one that triggers the most emotion.
Three basic checks can help eliminate a large part of questionable content.
They don't require any special skills.
The first: who says this?
It's not about blindly trusting certain media outlets, but about knowing whether the information comes from an identifiable source or an anonymous account.
Content that doesn't mention any author, date, or location should be treated with caution.
The second: when?
Many false pieces of information are actually true pieces of information taken out of their time.
An authentic photograph of a disaster that occurred ten years ago, republished as current news, can be very misleading.
The third: is it elsewhere?
If an important event really took place, several independent sources will report on it.
A major piece of information that exists only in one place is suspicious.
Additionally, there's a very simple tool for images: reverse image search, which allows you to find previous publications of a photo.
It takes just a few seconds.
Finally, a useful principle: we are all more gullible when it comes to what confirms our opinions.
The real difficulty is therefore not in verifying what others say.
It's in verifying what suits us.

sentences: We often oppose the city and nature, as if one excludes the other.
The reality is more nuanced and sometimes surprising.
Several studies show that some species — particularly wild bees and birds — are doing better today in certain cities than in the surrounding intensive agricultural areas.
This observation is not a compliment to the cities.
It is mainly a worrying signal regarding the countryside where hedges have disappeared and where treatments are intensive.
Cities do have real advantages.
They offer a great diversity of environments in a small space: gardens, parks, wastelands, rooftops, cemeteries, and the edges of railway tracks.
Flowering is spread out over a long period, while a field blooms all at once and then nothing.

They also have serious disadvantages: soil sealing, traffic, and especially nighttime lighting, which has a significant effect on insects and bats.

sentences: The disappearance of jobs is nothing new.
Lamp lighters, typists, and telephone operators existed, and then they no longer existed.
Each time, other jobs appeared, often in greater numbers.
This observation is used to reassure: automation does not destroy jobs, it displaces them.
In the long term, history tends to support this view.
But it overlooks two difficulties.
The first is the pace.
A transformation spread over fifty years is managed through generational renewal: children take on different jobs than their parents.
A transformation that occurs in ten years hits people in mid-career, who must retrain while managing family responsibilities and ongoing debt.
The second is geography.
The jobs that disappear and those that are created are not located in the same place.
When a factory closes in a medium-sized town, saying that jobs are being created in tech two hundred kilometers away doesn't help concretely.
What distinguishes countries that navigate these transitions well is not the speed of automation: it's the support.
Financed and anticipated training, maintained income during retraining, assistance with mobility.
Where this support is lacking, the consequences are felt long after: lasting unemployment, deterioration of health, political distrust.
The debate on artificial intelligence is today revisiting the same terms.
The useful question is probably not 'how many jobs will disappear?', because no one knows for sure.
It is: what will we have planned for those who held them?

sentences: Many people would like to get involved, help, contribute.
Few actually do.
Between intention and action, there is a recurring obstacle: the idea that a big gesture is needed, time that we don't have, a skill that we don't possess.
This requirement, seemingly commendable, is often what prevents starting.
Because the vast majority of what is done in associations does not require any rare skills.
Sorting clothes, accompanying an outing, managing a table at an event, making a phone call to an isolated person.
These are simple actions, within the reach of almost everyone.
And above all, what matters most is not the scale of the gesture, but the consistency and reliability.
A person who comes for two hours each week, whom you can count on, is worth more than a big burst of energy that fades after a month.
Those who get involved often share the same journey.
They started with very little, almost by chance, without much conviction.
Then they found meaning, connections, a place.
The commitment grew afterwards, but it started with a small step.
There is a more general lesson in this observation, applicable beyond volunteering.
Waiting for the right conditions, the right moment, the right cause, often leads to never starting.
Great things almost always arise from a modest beginning.
The opposite is also true: nothing collective exists if no one takes the first small step.
So the question is not 'Can I change things?'.
It is: 'Can I give two hours this week to something bigger than myself?'
That question almost always has an answer.

sentences: We feel like we freely choose what we watch.
We open an app, scroll, and click here rather than there.

However, this feeling of freedom masks a more complex reality: what we see has first been sorted, prioritized, and selected by systems that we do not control and that, most often, we do not understand.
Behind the apparent spontaneity of our choices, invisible decisions guide our gaze.
These decisions are far from trivial.
On major platforms, what appears first, what is highlighted, and what remains buried, results from rules designed by a few companies.
These rules determine which information reaches us, which opinions gain visibility, which voices are amplified, and which are silenced.
It is immense power, all the more formidable because it operates discreetly, without us perceiving it as power.
This power raises unprecedented democratic questions.
In a society, the way information circulates is never neutral: it shapes what citizens know, believe, and discuss.

Now this role, once held by institutions that were at least partially subject to public debate, is today largely exercised by private actors, driven by their own interests and largely escaping collective control.
A few companies effectively decide what billions of people see and do not see.
The problem is exacerbated by opacity.
The criteria that govern these choices are rarely made public; they are protected like industrial secrets.
We therefore endure decisions whose principles we are unaware of, unable to know why certain content is shown to us and why others are hidden.
This opacity makes any control, any criticism, almost impossible: one cannot discuss what one does not know.
What can we do in the face of this situation?
The first necessity is to become aware of it, because we do not distrust a power that we cannot see.
The second is to demand transparency: those who organize the circulation of information on such a large scale should be held accountable for the rules they apply.
The third is to refuse to rely on a single source and to deliberately diversify what informs us.
We believe we are looking at the world; most often, we are looking at what others have chosen to show us.
Knowledge does not make us entirely free, but it is the beginning of all freedom.

sentences: What does it mean to be healthy?
The most common answer is to say: not being sick.
According to this view, health would be a default state, one that we possess as long as no illness disturbs it.
This definition, seemingly obvious, is surprisingly poor, and it prevents us from properly thinking about what fundamentally constitutes a healthy life.
Reducing health to the absence of illness means defining it negatively, by what it is not.
But we can sense that health is more than that.
Two people can have no declared illness and be in very different states: one full of energy, the other exhausted; one calm, the other plagued by anxiety.
Neither is 'sick' in the strict sense, and yet one is doing well while the other is not.
Health, evidently, cannot be confined to merely the absence of pathology.
That is why a richer definition has been proposed, which sees health as a complete state of physical, mental, and social well-being.
This formulation has its flaws — such a complete state may never be fully achieved — but it has the merit of broadening our perspective.
It reminds us that health involves the body, but also the mind and social connections, and we cannot reduce it to just one of these aspects.
This broader conception has practical consequences.
If health is not just the absence of illness, then taking care of it does not only mean treating what is wrong, but also nurturing what is right.
Moving, sleeping, maintaining relationships, finding meaning, managing stress: all these dimensions are fully part of health, even though none appear on a prescription.
Taking care of oneself is more than just treating oneself.
However, we must be cautious of excess.
Making health an ideal of 'complete well-being' risks turning it into a permanent obligation, a demand to always be at our best.
But no one is at their best all the time, and feeling guilty for not achieving a perfect state would be a new form of distress.
Health is not a performance to achieve, but a balance to seek, always imperfectly.
Understanding that health goes beyond the absence of illness means stopping waiting to be sick to care about it.
It is recognizing that it is built every day, in the ordinary gestures of life, and not only at the doctor’s when something goes wrong.

sentences: No one can know everything or verify everything by themselves.
On the vast majority of topics, we are forced to rely on those who know: doctors, scientists, engineers, specialists of all kinds.
This trust in experts is inevitable and even reasonable: it would be absurd to claim to judge everything based solely on one's own opinion.
But it raises a delicate question: who to trust, and to what extent?
For experts are not infallible; they can make mistakes and sometimes contradict each other.
Let's start by dismissing two attitudes that are equally convenient and equally false.
The first is blind submission: believing an expert at their word simply because they are presented as such, without ever questioning.

The second is systematic distrust: rejecting the words of experts by principle, in the name of 'I form my own opinion,' which, due to a lack of expertise, is often just a poorly informed opinion disguised as independence of thought.
Between credulity and rejection, we must seek a more just path.
This path is based on a few guidelines.
First, competence is not general but specialized: an expert is only reliable in their own field.
An eminent scholar in one discipline has no more authority on another subject than anyone else.
Being wary of those who speak confidently outside their area of expertise is a healthy first reflex.
Notoriety is not competence, and the title of expert is only valid in the field where it was earned.
Next, we must distinguish between agreement and disagreement among experts.

When, on a question, the vast majority of specialists agree after years of work, that agreement constitutes the best available knowledge, and contradicting it based solely on one's intuition is unreasonable.
When, on the contrary, experts are genuinely divided, caution is necessary, and no one can claim to decide in the name of science.
Confusing a marginal disagreement with a genuine controversy, or presenting a consensus as merely an opinion, are two common ways to deceive.
Finally, we must question interests.
An expert is not a pure intellect: they can be influenced by what funds them, by their convictions, by the interests they serve.
This does not disqualify them — a funded researcher can be right — but it calls for vigilance, especially when their conclusions conveniently align with the interests of those who pay them.
Looking into who is speaking, and on whose behalf, is part of informed judgment.

Trusting experts is therefore neither an abdication nor naivety, provided it is done with discernment: respecting competence in its field, following solid consensus, remaining cautious in the face of disagreements, and questioning interests.
Thus, one can trust those who know without renouncing their own judgment — for true judgment does not consist of knowing everything oneself, but of reasonably knowing whom to trust.

sentences: The "common good" is one of those concepts that everyone invokes but no one defines.
Political leaders claim it, debates refer to it, and it serves as justification for all causes.
But in a divided society, made up of conflicting interests and incompatible notions of the good, does this concept still have any meaning?
Is there really a good that is common to all, or is it just an empty word, a flattering disguise for particular interests that present themselves as universal?
This question, which concludes our reflection on democracy, touches its foundation.
Skepticism regarding the common good has its reasons.
Our societies are deeply divided: the interests of some oppose those of others, the conceptions of what is good diverge, and what benefits some harms others.
In these conditions, talking about a "common good" seems to ignore real conflicts, masking opposing interests under a fiction of harmony.

Worse still, the invocation of the common good often serves to pass off a particular interest as the general interest: those who defend their advantages present them as the good of all, and the "common good" becomes the rhetorical weapon of the strongest or the most cunning.
Skepticism is therefore not wrong to be wary of such an easily distorted notion.
And yet, completely renouncing the idea of the common good would have dreadful consequences.

For if we admit that there is no common good, that society is merely a battlefield between irreconcilable particular interests, then politics becomes nothing more than a power struggle, where everyone seeks to impose their interest on others, and the only question is who will prevail.
There is no longer any deliberation on what would be just, only a struggle for power; no more reason, only force.
Denying the common good reduces political life to a war of all against all, where there is no longer any question of justice, only of domination.
How can we escape this alternative between a distorted notion and a destructive cynicism?
Perhaps by conceiving the common good differently than as a given harmony, a pre-established agreement on what is good.
The common good is not something that would exist ready-made, just waiting to be discovered; it is something to be built, to be sought together, through deliberation and compromise.
It is not the negation of particular interests and divisions, but the effort to find, despite them, what can be shared, what serves the whole beyond the interests of each.
The common good, in this sense, is not a fact, but a task, a horizon towards which we strive without ever fully reaching it.
This conception allows us to recognize divisions without renouncing the idea of a shared good.

Yes, interests oppose each other, conceptions of the good diverge; but there are also things that benefit everyone, or at least can be recognized by all as just after deliberation: peace, justice, equitable institutions, the preservation of what everyone depends on.
The common good is not what everyone would spontaneously agree on, but what an honest deliberation can recognize as transcending particular interests.
It does not eliminate conflicts, but it offers a horizon that transcends them, a criterion by which we can judge everyone's claims.
Affirming that the common good exists, not as a given but as a task, is therefore essential to democracy.
For democracy is not just the peaceful management of conflicts of interest; it is also the joint search for what is just, the deliberation on what serves the whole.
Without the idea of a good that transcends particular interests, it would reduce to bargaining among selfishness, to a struggle where numbers or force prevail.
With it, it becomes what it claims to be: the collective search, by free citizens, for what is good for all.

The common good may never be fully achieved, nor even definable once and for all; but to renounce it would be to renounce what distinguishes politics from mere war — and democracy from the simple domination of the majority.

sentences: There has always been a tension in the discussion about school, between two missions that are sometimes distinguished by two words: to instruct and to educate.
To instruct means to transmit knowledge, skills, and competencies; to educate means to shape individuals, develop judgment, impart values, and create accomplished human beings and citizens.
Should school limit itself to instruction, or does it also have a role in education?
This question, which may seem theoretical, actually involves opposing views on what school is and what it owes to those it welcomes.
One position argues that school should focus on instruction, the transmission of knowledge, and leave education in the broad sense to other entities — the family, society.
This position has its arguments.

School, it says, is legitimate in transmitting knowledge, an area where its authority is established; but shaping individuals and imparting values are choices that belong to families, and school should not replace them.
Wanting it to educate beyond instruction would give it excessive power over souls, risk indoctrination, and encroach on matters that do not concern it.
Let school instruct well, and let it leave the rest to those who are responsible for it.
This position, appealing in its modesty, nevertheless encounters a difficulty.
For can we really separate instruction from education, transmitting knowledge without shaping individuals?
Experience suggests not.
In transmitting knowledge, school also conveys, whether it wants to or not, ways of thinking, demands, and implicit values: rigor, a taste for truth, respect for facts, and the ability to reason.
Learning to seek the truth, to distinguish the true from the false, to argue, is not just about instruction; it is about forming oneself as a mind and as a person.
Instruction, when properly understood, is already a form of education; one does not transmit knowledge without shaping those to whom it is transmitted.
There is more.
Reducing school to mere instruction may overlook what is truly expected of it.
A society does not entrust its children to school merely for them to accumulate knowledge, but for them to become accomplished human beings, capable of thinking, judging, and living together.
School has always had, beyond instruction, a mission of formation: to create citizens, to transmit a common culture, and to develop autonomous judgment.

Renouncing this mission and limiting itself to instruction would impoverish school, reducing it to a technical function, forgetting what makes it an essential institution for the formation of individuals and communal life.
But the opposite position, which would make school the entity responsible for educating in the broadest sense, shaping individuals according to a certain model, also carries its dangers.
For educating implies choices — about values, about what constitutes a good life, about what an accomplished person should be — that are not neutral, and which a school cannot impose without risk.
Entrusting school with the task of shaping souls according to a given model risks indoctrination, uniformity, and encroachment on the freedom of conscience and the role of families.
A school that claims to educate in the fullest sense could become an instrument of conformity, which is the opposite of its true mission.
Wisdom may lie in a conception that transcends the alternative.
School should neither limit itself to instruction that pretends to transmit nothing but knowledge, nor claim an education that imposes a model of personhood.
Its own mission is to form free minds, capable of thinking for themselves, by transmitting the knowledge and demands that make this freedom possible.

To educate, for school, is not to shape according to a model, but to provide the means for self-formation; it is not to transmit values as dogmas, but to convey what allows for the judgment of values.
Understood this way, school instructs and educates at the same time, not by imposing a model, but by forming the very freedom of those it instructs — which may be its highest and most difficult task.

sentences: A human life is made up of a multitude of moments, experiences, and states that endlessly succeed one another, changing, often disparate.
And yet, we consider this succession to be a single, unified life, our own, endowed with a unity that makes it a whole rather than just a simple series of juxtaposed instants.
What creates this unity?
What connects the child I once was, the adult I am, and the old person I will be, into a single existence that is mine?
This question, an extension of our reflections on time and memory, touches on the mystery of what makes a life a life, and not just a dust of moments.
We have dismissed the idea of a substantial self, a fixed core that would remain identical amidst change; that is not where the unity of a life resides.
We have seen that the body changes, that consciousness transforms, and that memory itself constantly reconstructs the past.
Where then should we look for what unifies an existence?
The deepest answer may lie in a single word: the narrative.

What gives unity to a life is not a permanent substance, but a story; we connect the scattered moments of our existence by placing them within a narrative, giving them the form of a story that is ours, with its beginning, its unfolding, and its direction.
The unity of a life is a narrative unity.
This idea deserves to be explored.
We do not live our moments as a mere succession; we understand them by connecting them, by placing them within a framework, and by giving them meaning through their place in a story.
This event was a turning point; this one, a consequence of that one; this ordeal, a step towards what followed.
We continuously tell our life story, to ourselves and to others, narrating it, and it is through this narrative that the scattered moments become episodes of a single story.
The unity of our life is not given; it is constructed, woven by the incessant narrative we create, which connects what, without it, would be just a disjointed succession.
This narrative conception of identity sheds light on many things.
It explains why memory is so essential to our identity: because it provides the material for the narrative, preserving the past to connect it to the present.

It explains why we need to make sense of the events in our life, to understand them, to integrate them: because an event that remains senseless, unassimilable, would break the thread of the narrative, creating a blemish in the story.

It explains why the ordeals that make no sense, which we cannot integrate into our story, are so difficult to bear: they threaten the narrative unity, introducing a rupture into the narrative that we cannot fill.
To live is, in part, to tell one’s life, to weave it into a coherent story.
But this conception also has its limits and dangers, which must be acknowledged.
For the narrative we create of our life is a construction, and like any construction, it can be misleading.
We can tell ourselves a false story, deluding ourselves about the meaning of our life, imposing a false coherence onto the real disorder of our existence.
The need to make one’s life a coherent narrative can lead to falsification, simplification, and imposing meaning where there is none.

There is a possible tyranny of the narrative, which would suggest that every life must take the form of a well-constructed story, whereas many lives are made up of chance, discontinuity, and unconnected moments.
Recognizing the narrative unity of life should not lead to denying what existence has that is irreducibly scattered, contingent, and senseless.

Wisdom may consist in holding both: recognizing that we give our life a narrative unity, that we weave it into a story that constitutes it as ours, while at the same time not being deceived by this narrative, not sacrificing the truth of what we live, and accepting what our existence retains as irreducible to the narrative.
The thread of a life is not predetermined; we weave it, and this task is as much our freedom as it is our necessity.
But we must weave it with integrity, without deceiving ourselves, without imposing a false coherence on reality.

Making one’s life a true story, coherent without being artificial, unified without being falsified — that may be what it means to give meaning to one’s existence: not to discover a thread that preexists, but to weave one, patiently and honestly, that connects our moments without betraying what we have truly lived.

sentences: Some films, when they are released, go almost unnoticed, before becoming true cult films years later.
This phenomenon has always intrigued me.
How can a film fail commercially upon its release, then become, ten or twenty years later, an essential reference for an entire generation?
Several factors seem to explain this turnaround.
First, the audience was sometimes simply not ready for this type of story or tone, which was ahead of its time.
Then, discovering a forgotten film on television or, today, on a streaming platform allows it to find a completely new audience, without the pressure of box office expectations.
Finally, a cult film often builds around a community of fans who share their passion, quote lines to each other, and organize special screenings.
I myself discovered several of my favorite films long after their official release, thanks to recommendations from convinced friends.
The same phenomenon affects music: an album ignored at its release can, twenty years later, become a reference for an entire scene.

This gap between immediate reception and late recognition may say more about the audience's difficulty in appreciating what strays too far from their current expectations than about the actual quality of the work itself.
This phenomenon clearly shows that the value of a work is not measured solely by its immediate success.
Sometimes, it just takes the right moment and the right audience for a film to finally find its place.

sentences: Since I started working from home, the boundary between my work and personal life has become blurred.
Before, leaving the office really meant leaving work.
The commute home marked a clear transition between the two worlds.
Now, my computer stays on the kitchen table, visible all the time.
In the evening, while preparing dinner, I sometimes glance at new work messages, 'just to check.'
This constant availability has gradually settled in, without me consciously deciding to work more.
A message on Sunday evening, a quick reply over the weekend, a habit that builds up without us really noticing.
A friend, also working remotely, told me that he had to establish a strict rule: to completely put away his computer in a cupboard every evening, to physically mark the end of his workday.
I tried this method, with some success.
This simple gesture, almost symbolic, helps me to artificially recreate the boundary that the daily commute used to naturally create.

A colleague facing the same difficulty found his own solution, almost comical: he literally changes clothes at the end of the day, as if he were coming home from the office, just to mark a transition that the lack of a commute no longer provides.
Remote work gives us real freedom in how we organize our time.
But this freedom paradoxically requires a new discipline to prevent work from taking over every moment of our lives.

sentences: Living in an apartment without a garden, I thought composting was completely inaccessible to me.
While researching, I discovered a small indoor composter designed specifically for apartments, using worms to turn food waste into compost.
I admit, the idea initially grossed me out.
The thought of having worms in my kitchen didn't seem particularly appealing to me.
Despite this initial hesitation, I decided to give it a try, curious to see if it would really work in such a small space.

I had to learn, through trial and error, the right balance between wet waste and dry materials, like torn cardboard.
After several adjustments, the system ended up working well, with no noticeable odor, producing good quality compost that I now give to my neighbor who has a small garden.
My neighbors, curious to see this little composter on my countertop, asked me many questions; some eventually tried it themselves.
This gesture, which was purely personal at first, ended up spreading discreetly throughout the building, without me ever seeking it.

This experience, which seemed impossible at first in my small apartment, showed me that with a bit of research and patience, almost any ecological action can adapt, even to the most challenging living conditions.

sentences: In response to the growing criticism of fast fashion, a counter-movement is gaining traction: that of clothing designed to last several decades rather than just a few seasons, thus reviving a philosophy that was long dominant before the advent of mass industrial production.
This movement is based on an instructive historical observation.

Until the mid-twentieth century, buying a piece of clothing was a thoughtful investment, justifying a preference for quality materials and solid craftsmanship, even if it meant paying more at the initial purchase.

Supporters of this return to clothing durability put forward several converging arguments: a real cost per use that is often lower in the long term, despite a higher purchase price; a significantly reduced environmental impact; and a richer relationship with the item itself, which is maintained and sometimes repaired rather than simply replaced.
However, this philosophy faces significant structural obstacles.

The initial purchase price, often significantly higher than that of fast fashion, remains inaccessible for many consumers with modest incomes, which limits the real social reach of this movement, still largely associated with a wealthier clientele.

Moreover, the culture of rapid renewal, now deeply ingrained in our consumption habits and fueled by social media, does not easily disappear, even among consumers who are intellectually convinced by the arguments for sustainability.

Reconciling these two seemingly contradictory demands may represent the true challenge for the fashion industry in the years to come: making sustainable quality sufficiently accessible so that it ceases to be a luxury reserved for a few, without sacrificing the jobs of an industry that still supports millions of workers around the world.

sentences: Millions of readers immerse themselves each year in novels that they know full well do not reflect reality at all, whether they are fantastical tales, improbable romances, or epic adventures populated by imaginary creatures.
This practice, seemingly paradoxical, deserves our attention: why dedicate so much time and attention to stories whose fundamental unreality we recognize from the very first page?
One explanation lies in the escapist function that this acknowledged fiction precisely fulfills.

Unlike a supposedly realistic narrative, which could painfully remind us of the difficulties of everyday life, an openly fictional world offers a clearly defined mental space where the reader can temporarily take refuge without any possible confusion with their own existence.
A second, more subtle explanation concerns the ability of these unrealistic narratives to express, in a symbolic and distanced form, very real psychological or moral truths.

An imaginary world, precisely because it distances itself from reality, sometimes allows us to address universal questions — power, loyalty, sacrifice — with a clarity that the complexity of the real world would make more difficult to perceive directly.
This function of unrealistic fiction is not new: ancient myths and folk tales passed down for centuries already served a similar purpose, long before the advent of the modern novel.

Reading stories that we know are false probably does not simply amount to superficial entertainment, but rather meets an ancient and profound human need to understand our own condition through the reassuring detour of the imaginary.

sentences: What gains visibility in public debate depends less and less on a human editorial judgment that is accountable and responsible, and more and more on an opaque algorithmic calculation, the logic of which remains largely inaccessible even to those who experience its effects daily.
This almost silent substitution deserves our attention, as it profoundly alters the very conditions of collective deliberation.

Traditional journalism, despite its real limitations and biases, was based on an identifiable principle of responsibility: an editor-in-chief would choose, according to criteria that they could, in principle, explain and publicly defend, what deserved to be brought to the public's attention.
This human mediation, fallible but acknowledged, at least offered a critical perspective: one could contest an editorial line, identify its biases, and demand justification.
The algorithm that prioritizes our news feeds today does not meet any of these requirements.

It does not select based on an explicit conception of the public interest, but rather on a purely quantitative objective: to maximize the time of attention retained, the engagement measured in clicks, shares, and comments.

Whether this content informs, disinforms, calms, or exacerbates social tensions is, in a sense, perfectly indifferent to it, except to the extent that these effects influence the engagement it seeks to optimize.

This structural indifference produces a well-documented perverse effect: content that provokes outrage, fear, or scandal generally spreads more effectively than nuanced analyses, precisely because intense emotion encourages impulsive sharing, while nuance invites more silent reflection.

The algorithm, without any identifiable malicious intent, thus structurally favors a form of public debate that is more polarized, more simplified, and more conducive to confrontation than to genuine deliberation.

One could argue that platforms are not solely responsible for this outcome: after all, they merely exploit human tendencies that predate their existence, our longstanding attraction to scandal, controversy, and striking anecdotes.

This point is valid, but it does not dissolve the question of the responsibility that specifically falls on those who design these systems, knowingly, to exploit these tendencies on an unprecedented scale and with an effectiveness never seen before in the history of human communication.
This algorithmic opacity also raises a new issue of accountability: when a clearly problematic piece of content spreads widely, who is responsible for that spread?

Not the author of the content, who has merely exercised a legitimate freedom of expression, nor entirely the platform, which hides behind the supposed neutrality of its algorithm, as if it were a purely mechanical phenomenon, devoid of any identifiable intention and therefore of any truly assignable fault.

The central difficulty posed by this new configuration lies in its very opacity: unlike an editor-in-chief who could be challenged, questioned, or whose choices could at least be named, the algorithm remains a faceless arbiter, whose exact criteria are protected by commercial secrecy, and whose constant evolution makes any analysis quickly obsolete.

Demanding its regulation, as many observers suggest, requires resolving a difficult tension: how can we demand transparency from a mechanism whose relative opacity is precisely, in the eyes of those who exploit it, one of its main competitive advantages?
This question, still largely without a satisfactory answer, may define one of the major democratic challenges of our time.

sentences: When faced with a work that confuses us — an abstract painting, complex music, an obscure poem — a question often arises, tinged with a slight discomfort: must we understand it to appreciate it?
Many feel excluded from art because they do not 'understand', as if prior knowledge were necessary to have the right to feel.
This widespread belief does not hold up well under scrutiny, as it is based on a questionable conception of what it means to appreciate a work.
There is some truth in the idea that knowledge enriches experience.
Knowing the context of a work, the intentions of its author, and the codes of its time often allows us to perceive dimensions that would otherwise remain invisible.
An ancient religious painting is better appreciated by those who know its symbols; complex music is appreciated differently when we grasp its structure.
In this sense, understanding deepens pleasure, and ignorance can deprive us of much.
But making understanding a prerequisite for appreciation would be a mistake.
For many works touch us even before we understand them, and sometimes without us ever fully understanding them.
Music moves us without us knowing why; a poem captures us before we have unraveled its meaning; a painting holds us simply by its presence.
This immediate emotion, prior to any explanation, is a form of full appreciation that does not need to be justified by knowledge.
There is even something precious in this direct encounter, unmediated by commentary.
It reminds us that art speaks first to our sensitivity, not to our erudition; that it addresses something in us that precedes reasoning.
Reducing appreciation to understanding would mean forgetting this sensitive part and turning our relationship with art into an intellectual exercise reserved for those who know.
The danger of the belief that 'one must understand' is precisely here: it discourages, it intimidates, it distances from art those who, lacking knowledge, no longer dare to feel.
It transforms what should be a free encounter into an exam that one fears failing.
How many give up on entering a museum or listening to a demanding work, convinced that 'it's not for them'?
The truth is more welcoming: one can appreciate without understanding everything, feel without being able to explain, be touched without being able to justify it.
Knowledge can come later, deepen, enrich — and it is worth it.
But it is not the toll to pay to have the right to emotion.
In front of a work, the first thing to do is not to understand; it is to allow oneself to be touched.

sentences: While visiting a famous monument last summer, I noticed a behavior that made me think.
In front of me, a line of visitors was waiting their turn to take a specific photo, often the same one seen a thousand times on social media.
Once the photo was taken, most of them left almost immediately, without really looking at the monument itself.
This scene made me reflect on my own way of traveling.
How many times have I myself prioritized the perfect photo over the real experience of the moment?
I remember a recent trip where I spent almost twenty minutes trying to get the ideal photo of a sunset, instead of simply watching it, present, without a screen between us.

Some researchers who study modern tourism mention a phenomenon they call 'validation tourism': traveling more to prove to others on social media that we've been somewhere, rather than for the experience itself.
Some tourist sites are starting to limit this practice by banning selfie sticks or tightening visiting slots, specifically to encourage a more direct observation of the places.
These measures, still rare, may reflect an institutional awareness of the same issue I had observed in myself.
Since this awareness, I've been trying to limit my photos while traveling, sometimes forcing myself to put my phone away completely for a few hours.
It's not always easy, as the habit of photographing every moment has become automatic.
But I feel, when I succeed, a different, more real presence to what I came to see.

They went side by side, inseparably united.

sentences: Franz and the count got into the carriage, which was a coupe, Peppino sat next to Ali, and they set off at a gallop.

Ali had received orders in advance, as he took the street of the Cours, crossed the Campo Vaccino, went up the strada San-Gregorio, and arrived at the Saint-Sébastien gate; there the concierge wanted to make some difficulties, but the count of Monte-Cristo presented an authorization from the governor of Rome to enter and exit the city at any hour of the day or night; the drawbridge was therefore raised, the concierge received a louis for his trouble, and they passed.
The road the carriage was following was the ancient Appian Way, lined with tombs.

From time to time, in the light of the moon that was beginning to rise, Franz seemed to see a sentinel detach itself from a ruin, but immediately, at a signal exchanged between Peppino and this sentinel, it would return to the shadows and disappear.
A little before the Circus of Caracalla, the carriage stopped, Peppino came to open the door, and the count and Franz got out.
"In ten minutes," said the count to his companion, "we will have arrived."
Then he took Peppino aside, gave him a quiet order, and Peppino left after grabbing a torch that was taken from the trunk of the coupe.

Five more minutes passed, during which Franz saw the shepherd disappear down a small path amid the uneven terrain that forms the convulsed ground of the plain of Rome, and vanish into the tall reddish grasses that seem like the bristling mane of some gigantic lion.
"Now," said the count, "let's follow him."
Franz and the count also entered the same path which, after a hundred steps, led them down a slope into a small valley.
Soon they spotted two men talking in the shadows.
"Should we continue to advance?" Franz asked the count, "or should we wait?"
Let's go; Peppino must have informed the sentry of our arrival.
Indeed, one of these two men was Peppino, the other was a bandit on lookout.
Franz and the count approached; the bandit greeted them.
"Excellency," said Peppino, addressing the count, "if you would like to follow me, the entrance to the catacombs is just a short distance from here."

sentences: Mr. de Blacas ascended with the same speed as he had descended; but in the antechamber, he was forced to invoke the authority of the king.

Villefort's dusty outfit, his costume, which was completely inappropriate for court attire, had provoked the sensitivity of Mr. de Brézé, who was quite astonished to find this young man daring to appear dressed like that before the king.

But the duke resolved all difficulties with a single word: Order of His Majesty; and despite the comments that the master of ceremonies continued to make, for the sake of principle, Villefort was introduced.
The king was sitting in the same place where the duke had left him.
Upon opening the door, Villefort found himself directly in front of him: the first reaction of the young magistrate was to stop.
"Come in, Mr. de Villefort," said the king, "come in."
Villefort bowed and took a few steps forward, waiting for the king to question him.
"Mr. de Villefort," continued Louis XVIII, "here is the duke of Blacas, who claims that you have something important to tell us.
--Sire, the duke is right, and I hope that Your Majesty will recognize it himself.
--First, and above all, sir, is the situation as grave, in your opinion, as they want me to believe?
--Sire, I believe it is urgent; but, thanks to the diligence I have shown, it is not irreparable, I hope.

--Speak at length if you wish, sir," said the king, who was beginning to allow himself to be affected by the emotion that had disturbed Mr. de Blacas's face and altered Villefort's voice; "speak, and above all, start from the beginning: I like order in all things.
Sire, said Villefort, I will give Your Majesty a faithful report, but I must ask for your pardon if the trouble I am in casts some obscurity on my words.
A glance cast at the king after this insinuating preamble assured Villefort of the goodwill of his august listener, and he continued:

Sire, I arrived in Paris as quickly as possible to inform Your Majesty that I have discovered, in the course of my duties, not one of those vulgar and inconsequential plots that are hatched every day among the lower ranks of the people and the army, but a genuine conspiracy, a storm that threatens nothing less than the throne of Your Majesty.
Sire, the usurper is arming three ships; he is contemplating some project, perhaps insane, but possibly also terrible, as insane as it is.
At this hour, he must have left the island of Elba to go where? I do not know, but for sure to attempt a landing either in Naples, or on the coasts of Tuscany, or even in France.
Your Majesty is aware that the sovereign of the island of Elba has maintained relations with Italy and with France.

sentences: The departure.
The events that had just occurred were concerning all of Paris.

Emmanuel and his wife were recounting them, with a perfectly natural surprise, in their small living room on Rue Meslay; they were comparing these three catastrophes, as sudden as they were unexpected, involving Morcerf, Danglars, and Villefort.
Maximilien, who had come to pay them a visit, was listening to them or rather attending their conversation, immersed in his usual insensitivity.

"In truth," said Julie, "wouldn't one say, Emmanuel, that all these rich people, so happy yesterday, had forgotten, in the calculations on which they based their fortune, happiness, and reputation, the role of the evil genius, and that this one, like the wicked fairies from Perrault's tales who were neglected at some wedding or baptism, suddenly appeared to take revenge for this fatal oversight?
--What disasters!" said Emmanuel, thinking of Morcerf and Danglars.
--What suffering!" said Julie, recalling Valentine, whom, by a woman's instinct, she did not want to name in front of her brother.

--If it is God who has struck them," said Emmanuel, "it is because God, who is supreme goodness, found nothing in the past of these people that deserved a mitigation of their punishment; it is because these people were cursed.
--Aren't you being rather reckless in your judgment, Emmanuel?" said Julie.
When my father, gun in hand, was ready to blow his brains out, if someone had said, as you say now, 'This man deserved his punishment,' wouldn't that person have been mistaken?
--Yes, but God did not allow our father to succumb, just as He did not allow Abraham to sacrifice his son.
To the patriarch, as to us, He sent an angel who cut halfway the wings of Death."
He had barely finished saying these words when the sound of the bell rang out.
It was the signal given by the concierge that a visitor was arriving.
Almost at the same moment, the door of the living room opened, and the Count of Monte Cristo appeared on the threshold.
It was a double cry of joy from the two young men.
Maximilien lifted his head and let it fall back down.

sentences: But what was this part of the globe submerged by cataclysms?
Who had arranged these rocks and stones like dolmens from prehistoric times?
Where was I, where had the fancy of Captain Nemo taken me?
I would have liked to question him.
Not being able to do so, I stopped him.
I grabbed his arm.
But he, shaking his head and pointing to the last peak of the mountain, seemed to say to me:
"Come! come again! come always!"
I followed him in one last surge, and in a few minutes, I had climbed the peak that rose about ten meters above all this rocky mass.
I looked at the side we had just crossed.
The mountain rose only seven to eight hundred feet above the plain; but from its opposite slope, it towered twice as high over the bottom below this part of the Atlantic.
My gaze extended far and encompassed a vast space illuminated by a violent flash.
Indeed, this mountain was a volcano.
Fifty feet below the peak, amidst a rain of stones and cinders, a large crater was spewing torrents of lava, which cascaded like fire within the liquid mass.
Positioned this way, this volcano, like an immense torch, illuminated the lower plain to the farthest limits of the horizon.

sentences: I started collecting vinyl records five years ago.
Today, I have about two hundred.
It all started at my parents' house.
While clearing out the attic, I found a box with my father's records: jazz and French songs.
I bought an old second-hand turntable, and I listened to those records one Sunday afternoon.
It surprised me.
The sound wasn't perfect, there were some little noises, but the listening experience was different.
With a vinyl record, you can't skip from one song to another in a second.
You have to get up, turn the record over.
You listen to the whole album, in order.
Since then, I've been looking for records everywhere: flea markets, thrift shops, small second-hand stores.
It's a pleasure in two parts.
First, the search: we look at hundreds of covers, often finding nothing.
Then, sometimes, the discovery.
Last month, at a flea market, I found an album I had been looking for for two years.
It cost three euros.
I was so happy that the seller laughed.
My friends sometimes tell me, "You can listen to everything for free on the internet."
That's true.
But it's not the same thing.
On Sunday evenings, I put on a record, and I do nothing else.

sentences: There is a cultural difference that Tom often talks about: the way to queue.
In the United Kingdom, queuing is almost sacred.
People naturally line up behind one another.
Cutting in front of someone is considered very serious.
In France, queuing exists too, of course.
But it is often less straight and less strict.
At the bakery, for example, people tend to form a small group.
The first time, Tom found it chaotic.
He thought that no one knew who had arrived first.
Then he observed, and he understood that he was mistaken.
People know perfectly well whose turn it is.
They watch each other, and often someone says: "It's your turn, madam, I believe."
There is an important rule to know.
In a small shop, you have to ask: 'Who is the last?'
This question solves everything, without a straight line.
Tom took some time to learn it.
At first, he politely stayed near the door, and people entered after him and went ahead.
He waited without being served.
'No one was dishonest,' he says now.
'It's just that I hadn't said I was there.'
Two cultures, two methods.
In both cases, the idea is the same: everyone takes their turn.

sentences: The freedom of some ends where the freedom of others begins.
This formula, often quoted, seems to resolve in one word the problem of the limits of freedom.
Everyone would be free to do what they want, as long as they do not infringe on the freedom of others.
The idea is correct in principle, and it expresses a fundamental requirement: no one has the right to crush another's freedom in the name of their own.
But as soon as we try to apply it, we realize that it shifts the difficulty more than it resolves it.
Because the whole question is to know where, precisely, my freedom infringes on that of others.
Let's consider simple cases: they are rare.
Hitting someone, stealing from them, coercing them: these are obvious infringements on the freedom of others, which no one disputes.
But the vast majority of our actions have less direct, more diffuse effects on others, which can be debated endlessly.
My way of living, consuming, and expressing myself affects others in a thousand indirect ways.
At what point does this effect constitute an infringement on their freedom, which would justify limiting mine?
The formula does not say; it assumes resolved what is precisely problematic.
Let's take an example.
Am I free to harm my own health if it only concerns me?
One might be tempted to answer yes, in the name of my freedom over myself.
But my choices have consequences for others: for my loved ones, for a community that may have to care for me, for the example I set.
Where does what only concerns me end, and where does what concerns others begin?
The boundary, far from being clear-cut, is the very subject of political and moral debate.
There's more.
Liberties often conflict with each other, without any one clearly encroaching on the other.
My freedom of expression may clash with another's right not to be defamed; my freedom to undertake may conflict with others' freedom to live in a healthy environment.
These conflicts cannot be resolved by drawing a simple boundary, as they involve two equally legitimate freedoms that limit each other.
We then need to arbitrate, weigh, and decide which one must yield, and to what extent — something that the formula cannot tell us.
That's why the question of the limits of freedom cannot be resolved by a formula, but through ongoing deliberation.

A society must constantly decide, on a thousand topics, where to set the boundaries: which freedoms to absolutely protect, which to limit in the name of others or the common good, and how to arbitrate between competing freedoms.
These decisions are never definitive; they are re-discussed in every era, as customs and techniques change.
The beautiful formula about the freedom of some and others is therefore not false; it is merely the beginning of the problem, not its solution.

It reminds us of an essential principle — that my freedom is not unlimited, that it must coexist with that of others — but it leaves us with the difficult task: to draw, case by case, the boundary that it merely names.
Living freely together means accepting to endlessly re-discuss this boundary, rather than believing that a phrase could fix it once and for all.
